prompt:
Research what the Python Software Foundation or the CPython developers have officially said about the performance impact of the free-threaded (no-GIL) build. Cite the PEP or documentation page and quote the relevant statement.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

If you're not sure about something, just say so.

response.content:
Based on the provided search results, here are the official statements from the Python Software Foundation and CPython developers regarding the performance impact of the free-threaded (no-GIL) build:

SOURCE: https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html | QUOTE: "The free-threaded build has additional overhead when executing Python code compared to the default GIL-enabled build. The amount of overhead depends on the workload and hardware. On the pyperformance benchmark suite, the average overhead ranges from about 1% on macOS aarch64 to 8% on x86-64 Linux systems." | CLAIM: Official Python documentation acknowledging the single-threaded performance overhead of the free-threaded build and providing current benchmark figures.
SOURCE: https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html | QUOTE: "The free-threaded build will typically use more memory compared to the default build. There are multiple reasons for this, mostly due to design decisions." | CLAIM: Official Python documentation acknowledging increased memory usage in the free-threaded build.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "the performance penalty on linear performance, comparing a free-threaded build against a with-GIL build, as measured by the pyperformance benchmarks (for example as run by Microsoft’s Faster CPython team, or Meta’s Python Runtime team), is currently around 10% (except on macOS, where it’s more like 3%)." | CLAIM: PEP 779 reports the current single-threaded performance penalty of the free-threaded build as measured by benchmark teams.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "We have a few more PRs in flight that should get us comfortably below 10% on Linux and Windows." | CLAIM: PEP 779 indicates that active development is underway to further reduce the performance penalty below 10%.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "free-threaded Python currently sees about 15-20% higher memory use (geometric mean, as measured by pyperformance)." | CLAIM: PEP 779 quantifies the increased memory usage of the free-threaded build.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "Realistically, though, higher memory use is the cost of having efficient, safe free-threading, and we are unlikely to get this very close to the with-GIL build’s memory use without significant performance cost." | CLAIM: PEP 779 establishes that higher memory usage is an expected, inherent trade-off for safe and efficient free-threading.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "The Steering Council mentioned they expected free-threaded Python to be around 10-15% slower, although this was not a hard target. We are currently around 10% and don’t expect it to get slower, but for phase II (not the default flip), we propose 15% as a hard performance target." | CLAIM: PEP 779 references the Steering Council's expectations for the performance penalty and proposes a hard target for the "officially supported" phase.
SOURCE: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-703-making-the-global-interpreter-lock-optional-in-cpython-acceptance/37075?u=hugovk | QUOTE: "Regarding the expected performance impact of the free-threaded build, the SC thinks a significant performance penalty is expected in a free-threaded build, and the benefit is probably worth that price. At this point we’re expecting a (worst case) performance penalty of 10-15%." | CLAIM: The Python Steering Council's official acceptance of PEP 703 acknowledges a 10-15% expected worst-case performance penalty and deems it an acceptable trade-off.
SOURCE: https://discuss.python.org/t/pep-703-making-the-global-interpreter-lock-optional-in-cpython-acceptance/37075?u=hugovk | QUOTE: "The performance impact should be isolated to a free-threaded build; a GIL build should not see any performance impact in existing code." | CLAIM: The Steering Council mandates that performance regressions must be contained to the free-threaded build, leaving the default GIL-enabled build unaffected.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "The changes to make CPython thread-safe without the GIL increase execution overhead for `--disable-gil` builds. The performance impact is different for programs that use only a single thread compared to programs that use multiple threads" | CLAIM: PEP 703 establishes that disabling the GIL introduces execution overhead and notes a variance between single-threaded and multi-threaded performance impacts.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "For thread-safety reasons, an application running with multiple threads will only specialize a given bytecode once; this is why the overhead for programs that use multiple threads is larger compared to programs that only use one thread." | CLAIM: PEP 703 explains a specific technical reason for increased overhead in multi-threaded programs due to bytecode specialization limitations.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "The largest contribution to execution overhead is biased reference counting followed by per-object locking." | CLAIM: PEP 703 identifies the specific technical mechanisms most responsible for the performance overhead.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "Note that this PEP would not affect the performance of the default (non `--disable-gil`) builds of CPython." | CLAIM: PEP 703 reaffirms that the default interpreter build will experience no performance impact from these changes.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "However, with the GIL disabled, programs that use multiple threads should also be able to more effectively use multiple CPU cores." | CLAIM: PEP 703 highlights the primary performance benefit of the free-threaded build, which is the ability to utilize multiple CPU cores efficiently.
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: The exact rationale for why the performance overhead is lower on macOS aarch64 (around 1-3%) compared to Linux and Windows x86-64 (around 8-10%), beyond general statements that it "depends on the workload and hardware."
